# Deploy: finish or roll back an interrupted deploy

## Why
A deploy killed while draining (SIGTERM/SIGINT) left the release checkout at the new commit, already installed and checked, and the daemon still on the old code in `draining` state. Queued runs were then blocked indefinitely. Re-running `deploy` printed `already at <sha>` and returned, because it compares the target to the checkout rather than to the running daemon.

## Design
- `/api/health` reports the commit the daemon booted from (`sha`, read once at startup).
- `deploy` compares the target to the running daemon's `sha`, not the checkout. If the checkout already matches the target but the daemon runs another commit, continue from "gates passed": drain, wait, restart. If the daemon is draining and nothing is deploying, say so and resume it or continue.
- Install SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers for the duration of a deploy. Before the restart, roll back the checkout and resume the scheduler, then exit non-zero. After the restart, just exit.
- `deploy` prints the daemon `sha` before and after.

## Acceptance
- Tests with the injectable `command`/`client`/`restart`:
  - checkout at target with the daemon on the previous sha → drains and restarts;
  - both at target → "already deployed", no restart;
  - a signal during the drain wait → checkout restored and resume requested;
  - health includes `sha`.
- `bun run check` passes; under ~200 lines.

# Cost display hides subscription-equivalent work behind sub-cent metered spend

## Why
Since triage moved to OpenRouter (`gpt-6-luna`, about $0.0002 per run), every run has a tiny metered cost. Every cost cell uses the rule "show `costUsd` if > 0, else `≈costEquivUsd`", so recent runs display `$0.000` and hide $3–$19 of subscription-equivalent work. This affects:
- the runs table (`ui/components/RunsTable.tsx`)
- the invocations table (`ui/components/InvocationsTable.tsx`)
- the dashboard model cards (`ui/pages/Dashboard.tsx`)
- the Models page (`ui/pages/Models.tsx`)
- `limitless ls` (`src/cli/main.ts`)

Also, `CostChart` stacks `costUsd + costEquivUsd`, but `costEquivUsd` already includes metered invocations (their equivalent equals their real cost), so metered spend is counted twice.

## Semantics (keep the data model)
- `costUsd` = real money paid (metered providers).
- `costEquivUsd` = what all of the run's work would cost at API list prices, including the metered part.

## Design
- One shared pure formatter, used by the UI and the CLI (for example `src/core/cost-format.ts`): `formatCost(costUsd, costEquivUsd)` returns `{ primary, paid, title }`.
  - `primary` = `≈$<equiv>` (the work done).
  - `paid` = `$<costUsd>` only when `costUsd` ≥ $0.005 (displays as at least $0.01), otherwise null.
  - `title` gives both exact values (e.g. `API-equivalent $4.34 · paid $0.0002`).
  - Cells render `primary`, plus `paid` in bold when present. When there is no equivalent and no cost, show `—`.
- `CostChart`: stack metered (`costUsd`) and subscription/local (`costEquivUsd − costUsd`, clamped at 0), so the bar height equals `costEquivUsd`. Tooltip wording matches.
- `KpiStrip` and provider cards: make sure totals use the same semantics (no double counting).

## Acceptance
- Unit tests for `formatCost`:
  - sub-cent paid plus a large equivalent shows the equivalent only, with both values in the title;
  - ≥ 1¢ paid shows both;
  - zero/zero shows `—`;
  - local-only work shows `≈$0.00` or `—` consistently.
- Chart stack test: a day with metered $0.19 and equivalent $6.75 has a bar total of $6.75.
- `limitless ls` shows `≈$4.34` for a run with $0.0002 paid.
- `bun run check` passes; under ~250 lines.

# Gates under parallel load: machine-wide gate slots and flaky retry

## Why
Every run runs the full gate suite (Limitless: `bun run check`, about 1 minute of CPU) on the same machine, as do verify sandboxes and eval trials. Several concurrent suites contend for CPU. Tests with short timeouts then fail spuriously, and a spurious "regressed" gate costs a whole implement round. A verifier recently observed timeout failures in the suite that reproduced on the base commit only under load.

## Design
- **Gate slots.** A process-wide semaphore around `runGates` (setup and checks), `max_concurrent_gates` in config (default: max(1, floor(cpu cores / 4))). Waiting for a slot emits a single event. Baseline gates in `prepare` use the same slots.
- **Flaky retry.** When a check fails, the same check passed on the baseline, and the output doesn't point at files the change touched, re-run that check once inside a slot. A pass on retry gives verdict `flaky` (non-blocking, surfaced as a warning in the report, with both outputs kept). A fail stays blocking. Retries are recorded so flaky tests can be listed and fixed.
- **`GateVerdict`** gains `flaky`. The report and UI render it; `compareGates` stays pure (retry happens in the gates stage).

## Acceptance
- Unit tests:
  - the semaphore bounds concurrent gate processes;
  - fail → retry → pass gives `flaky` and doesn't block;
  - fail → retry → fail blocks;
  - a check already failing on the baseline is not retried.
- `bun run check` passes; under ~300 lines.

# Conflict-resolution round must produce a real merge commit (factory merges, agent resolves)

## Bug
Run mukacfa88tqj (#61, PR #81): the delivery rebase conflicted, so the engine scheduled a resolution round whose feedback tells the implementer to `git merge origin/<base>` and resolve. The resulting commit `efb08dd` was a **single-parent** commit containing 1,442 lines of `main`'s changes across 21 files. The merge parent was lost, probably because the agent sandbox can't write the worktree's git metadata (it lives outside the worktree), so the agent applied `main`'s changes by hand.

Effects:
- GitHub showed other PRs' work as this PR's changes (38 files instead of 19), which misleads review.
- If `main` has moved further on those files, landing risks conflicts or confusing 3-way merges.
- The orchestrator had to reconstruct the merge by hand.
Parallel runs make delivery conflicts common, so this recurs.

## Design
- The **factory** performs the merge in the worktree (it has permission to write git metadata): `git merge --no-ff --no-commit origin/<base>` with hooks disabled and the scrubbed env.
  - Clean: commit it as a merge commit (two parents), re-run gates and continue to delivery; no agent needed.
  - Conflicted: leave conflict markers and `MERGE_HEAD` in place. The resolution round tells the agent: "resolve the conflict markers in these files, preserving both intents; do not run git". The factory then verifies no markers remain, stages, and commits with `MERGE_HEAD` (a real merge commit).
- If the agent's result has no `MERGE_HEAD`, or the commit has fewer than two parents, fail the round with a clear error instead of delivering.
- The audit and review diff for the resolution round is against the new base tip, so reviewers see the resolution, not `main`'s changes.
- Reuse the same helper for #46's refresh runs.

## Acceptance
- Real-git tests (temp repos, no network):
  - a conflicting base advance produces a two-parent merge commit on the run branch, with conflicts resolved by a fake agent editing files only;
  - a clean advance merges without an agent round;
  - an agent result without a merge parent fails the round;
  - the PR diff (`git diff base...branch`) contains only the run's own changes.
- `bun run check` passes; under ~350 lines.

# Never strand verified work: deliver a draft PR when post-verify steps fail

## Why
Run mukehly9lr4a (#86) passed verify 16/16 in round 3. Its delivery merge then conflicted, the resolution round failed, and the run ended needs-human **without pushing or opening a PR**. The verified work existed only in the run's worktree, and the orchestrator had to recover it by hand (PR #96).

## Design
- When a run has a passing verify (or, for `quick`, an approving review) at some commit, and any later step fails (delivery merge, conflict-resolution round, post-merge gates), deliver a **draft PR** from the last verified commit:
  - title prefixed `[needs human]`, report attached;
  - a clear section: "Verified at `<sha>`; failed after verification at `<stage>`: `<reason>`. The PR may conflict with `<base>`."
- Record `lastVerifiedSha` in run state whenever verify passes; delivery uses it on the failure path.
- For existing-branch (Dependabot) runs, never push on the failure path, as today.
- #46's refresh runs can then pick up a conflicting draft.

## Acceptance
- Fake-harness tests:
  - verify passes, then a conflict round fails: a draft PR is created from `lastVerifiedSha` with the failure explained, and the run is needs_human with `prUrl` set;
  - a failure before any passing verify behaves as today;
  - a Dependabot existing-branch run never pushes on this path.
- `bun run check` passes; under ~250 lines.

# M4.5: Review quality: research-first redesign of the review stage

Review is the main defence against deep bugs piling up in factory-written code, and it should be the best defect finder we can afford. Today the review stage is a single reviewer with a blocker/major/minor rubric. Its eval (15 cases) found no model that clears the defect-recall floor (0.5 Wilson lower bound), and orchestrator-side review agents keep finding real bugs after factory review has passed a PR.

This milestone comes before the rest of M5.

## Phases
1. **Research.** Recent literature and benchmarks on LLM defect detection. Industry systems (multi-agent/specialised reviewers, adversarial framing, cross-vendor ensembles, validation passes, dedup, severity ranking). Our own escaped defects. Output: `docs/research/08-code-review.md`.
2. **Review eval v2.** Real escaped defects reconstructed as cases (base + buggy diff + hidden reproduction), plus clean controls. Metrics: recall by severity, false findings per clean case, cost and latency. It evaluates review *systems* (panels, prompts, schedules), not just single models.
3. **Design.** A reviewer panel, finding dedup and severity classification (critical/high/medium/low), finding validation, and a deterministic convergence schedule. Candidate schedule: round 1 fixes all findings, round 2 fixes high and critical, round 3 fixes critical only. Control flow stays deterministic code.
4. **Build.** Factory-built PRs, each gated by the eval showing an improvement over the current single reviewer at acceptable cost.
5. **Demo.**

Sub-issues are filed once the research is done.

# Failure injection part 1: restarts mid-stage and harness/provider faults

M5 "failure-injection tests". `test/hardening.test.ts` covers process handling, the audit and a few pipeline edges. It does not systematically check that the factory ends in a correct, resumable state when things fail mid-run.

## Design
- **A fault seam for tests only.** `deps.faults?: FaultPlan` maps named points to an injected action (`throw`, `hang until aborted`, `kill`). Points include `stage:<name>:before`, `stage:<name>:after`, `harness:invoke`, `harness:stream` (malformed or truncated output) and `store:save`. It is a no-op when absent, and production never sets it.
- **Scenarios**, each asserting the persisted end state (run status, stage rows, state_json, invocations, worktree present, no duplicate side effects):
  1. **Daemon restart mid-stage** (abort plus a fresh `Factory` on the same DB) during implement, gates, review, verify and deliver. The run resumes at the start of that stage with the same round and implementer, and nothing is applied twice (no second commit or PR).
  2. **Harness faults:** non-zero exit, killed process, malformed/truncated stream JSON, a timeout, and structured output failing its schema. The run retries or falls back per policy and records each attempt, or ends `needs_human` with a clear reason; never `failed` with an internal error.
  3. **Provider faults:** 429/quota rejection mid-invocation leads to a cooldown and fallback to the next candidate; every candidate unavailable gives `NoCapacityError`, surfaced as a clear run error; a provider disabled while a stage runs doesn't affect the running invocation but is honoured for the next.
  4. **Cancellation during each stage:** the run ends `cancelled`, the process group is killed, and the worktree is kept for GC.
- The fake harness gains the scripted fault behaviours it needs.

## Acceptance
- One test per scenario; everything runs with fakes. No real LLM, network or `gh`.
- `bun run check` passes; under ~700 lines, mostly tests.

# Conflict-free migrations for parallel branches

## Why
`src/db/migrations.ts` is one array with sequential `version` integers. Two parallel runs that each add a migration both append `version: N+1` at the end of the same array, so every such pair conflicts, and the orchestrator has renumbered by hand several times (v5–v12).

## Design
- One file per new migration: `src/db/migrations/<UTC timestamp>-<slug>.sql`, e.g. `20260927T1500-run-dependencies.sql`. Files load at startup (`readdirSync`, sorted by filename) and are applied in order inside a transaction each.
- Track applied migrations by name in a `schema_migrations(name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, applied_at INTEGER)` table. On first start after this change, record the existing array migrations 1..N (named `legacy-0001-<name>`...) as applied according to the current `user_version`. The legacy array stays frozen and append-only rules move to the directory.
- The directory must never contain two files with the same name; tests fail if a file is edited after it ships (keep a checked-in hash list, `src/db/migrations/SHIPPED`, which the test compares).
- Update AGENTS.md: "New persisted fields need a new file in `src/db/migrations/`".

## Acceptance
- Tests:
  - a fresh DB applies legacy plus directory migrations;
  - an existing DB at `user_version = N` applies only new files;
  - two files added on different branches apply in filename order regardless of merge order;
  - an edited shipped file fails the test.
- Starting the daemon on a copy of the production DB is a no-op except the new table. The orchestrator verifies this before deploy.
- `bun run check` passes; under ~300 lines.

# Concurrency limits from config, and parallel slots for local models

## Why
Provider concurrency (`claude` 3, `codex` 3, `openrouter` 4, local 1) is hard-coded in the catalog, and `max_concurrent_runs` defaults to 3. The owner has plenty of subscription capacity, so these limits (not quota) cap throughput. Local servers may also sustain more than one request with batched decoding.

## Design
- `[providers.<id>] max_concurrent = N` in config.toml overrides `ProviderDef.maxConcurrent`, validated as a positive integer. Unknown provider ids are a config error. `limitless providers` shows the effective limit.
- Keep the defaults unchanged in code. The owner's config raises them.

  - Record results in docs/research.
